reading.title: Drafting the Seventh-Grade Charter
reading.purpose: Listen to two classmates debate how to design fair rules for a simulated island nation.
paras: "If we have to govern this imaginary island for social studies, we should keep it simple," Malik said, tapping his pencil on the map. "One ruler makes every choice, like a monarchy where a king or queen holds power for life. No endless meetings."

"Simple for the ruler, maybe," Sofia replied, sliding a blank chart between them. "What if that leader decides to oppress the islanders, treating them harshly and shutting down any complaint? Without checks, citizens lose their liberty, their freedom to speak and make daily choices."

"Fair point," Malik admitted. "Then let us build a republic instead, where voters elect representatives to make decisions for them. We can set up a small legislature, a council of elected lawmakers, to write and update rules when the island grows."

"Good," Sofia said, sketching three boxes on the chart. "Now what about our neighbors across the bay? Since our island is sovereign, holding the highest authority over its own territory, nobody else can tell us how to run our ports. Still, we should sign a treaty, a formal written agreement between both islands, so fishing boats share the water peacefully."

"I like that," Malik said. "Let us also write a clear policy on how to handle storms and food storage, so every town follows the same plan. And what if a rule stops working after five years?" Sofia grinned and added a final box at the bottom. "We should plan for change too. We include a path for reform, a peaceful way to improve any law that turns out to be unfair. That way our island stays steady without freezing in place."

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "sovereign" most nearly means
choices: sharing every port rule with a neighboring island
holding the highest authority over its own land
changing its written laws every single year
letting a single king decide who may go fishing
qs.why: Sofia defines sovereign right in the sentence as "holding the highest authority over its own territory."

qs.q: Which sentence explains how the students make sure unfair laws can be fixed later?
choices: Let us also write a clear policy on how to handle storms and food storage, so every town follows the same plan.
And what if a rule stops working after five years?
Sofia grinned and added a final box at the bottom.
We include a path for reform, a peaceful way to improve any law that turns out to be unfair.
qs.why: This sentence directly states their safeguard for changing unfair laws: a peaceful path for reform.

ev.text: We include a path for reform, a peaceful way to improve any law that turns out to be unfair.

qs.q: Why does Malik give up his first idea of a monarchy?
choices: He realizes one unchecked ruler could harm citizens and take away their freedom.
He remembers that the social studies rubric forbids writing about kings or queens.
He wants to avoid signing any fishing agreement with the neighboring island.
He thinks a council of elected lawmakers will never need to hold long meetings.
qs.why: After Sofia warns that a single ruler could oppress citizens and remove their liberty, Malik agrees and proposes a republic.

qs.q: What is the main focus of Malik and Sofia's conversation?
choices: Drawing a detailed map of fishing routes and storm shelters around a real island.
Comparing different ways to structure a fair, self-ruling government for a project.
Proving that a monarchy is always faster and safer than an elected council.
Debating whether neighbors across the bay should be allowed to visit their ports.
qs.why: The dialogue walks through monarchy, republic, legislature, treaties, policy, and reform as the students design a fair charter.

clues.text: where a king or queen holds power for life
their freedom to speak and make daily choices
a formal written agreement between both islands
